titleText.es: En su momento, programar a los robots sexuales para que disfrutaran del sexo pareció una medida sensata, pero no nos dimos cuenta de las consecuencias del desarrollo de sus fetiches.
titleText.en: Programming the sexbots to enjoy sex seemed a sensible move at the time, but we didn't realize the consequences of their developing fetishes.
titleText.noteEn: The English text is the official xkcd title text; the Spanish archive expands sexbots to robots sexuales. The Spanish raster omits the official GRAB sound, changes official NOM to Spanish ÑAM, and leaves PLINK and KZZZT untranslated. Vision misread those visible sounds as PENt, NAM, and KZZZ2T, and it missed the written accent in QUÍTATE; this artifact follows the raster, teaches ÑAM, and excludes only the two untranslated sounds.

applications.explanationEn: Mira is mirar's positive command for one familiar listener.
Nueva comes before novia and presents the person as newly in the role or relationship, rather than describing her as newly made.
Nueva uses the feminine singular ending -a to match the feminine singular noun novia.
Novia names the person, and androide follows it to describe what kind of girlfriend she is.
Robot names the thing, and the describing word sexual follows it in the neutral order.

excludedUnits.rationale: PLINK is an untranslated comic-book impact sound, not a Spanish lexical word.
KZZZT is an untranslated electrical sound effect rather than Spanish vocabulary.

regions.labelEs: NO CREO QUE SOLDAR AL ARCO UN RABITO DE CEREZA CUENTE COMO SEXY.

applications.exampleEs: NO CREO QUE SOLDAR AL ARCO UN RABITO DE CEREZA CUENTE
applications.explanationEn: No makes creo negative, que introduces the doubted idea, and ordinary cuenta changes to cuente because the speaker does not present that classification as a fact.
Soldar names the welding action, and al arco identifies the electric-arc method.
Cuente supplies the doubted form of contar, como introduces the category, and sexy fills that category slot.
Quita is quitar's positive command for one familiar listener, with te attached for quitarse.
Te attaches to the end of the positive command quita, and the written accent preserves the command's original stress.
The attached te identifies the wearer, so los introduces the plural clothing item without a separate possessive.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: una nueva persona o cosa · una persona o cosa nueva
cards.questionEn: What difference can the position of nuevo make?
cards.answerEn: Before the person or thing, nuevo often means newly added or newly in that role; after it, nuevo more often stresses that the thing itself is brand-new.
cards.noteEn: Nuevo changes to nueva, nuevos, or nuevas to match what it describes. Una nueva compañera usually means someone who has recently become a coworker or classmate. Una mesa nueva more often means a newly made or unused table. Context can blur the contrast, so this is a common tendency rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.answerEn: is; belongs to the stated category
cards.noteEn: Es is the present form of ser used for one person or thing. Between two naming words, it identifies or classifies the first as the second.
Ñam is a common Spanish sound for taking a bite or eating eagerly. Repeating it suggests repeated bites.

example.es: El niño miró el pastel y dijo: «¡Ñam!».
example.en: The child looked at the cake and said, “Yum!”

cards.questionEn: What verb form usually follows a negative belief such as “I do not think that…”?
cards.answerEn: After the negative belief and que, use the form that presents the idea as doubted rather than asserted as fact.
cards.noteEn: For many verbs, this form has a changed ending: habla becomes hable, and comen becomes coman. A positive belief normally uses the ordinary fact-stating form instead.

example.es: No creo que Ana esté aquí.
example.en: I do not think Ana is here.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “to arc-weld” or “to weld using an electric arc”?
cards.noteEn: Al combines a and el inside this conventional technical expression. Arco names the bright electrical discharge whose heat melts metal. Soldar changes for the person and time, while al arco stays unchanged.

cards.answerEn: with; by means of the (a + el, introducing a method)
cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a and el. In some technical expressions, it introduces the tool or process used, as in al láser and al arco.

example.es: La pieza se cortó al láser.

cards.noteEn: In welding, arco is the bright electrical discharge that supplies intense heat. This is different from arco meaning a bow or a curved arch.

example.es: El arco eléctrico produce mucho calor.
example.en: The electric arc produces a great deal of heat.

cards.noteEn: Rabito adds the ending -ito to rabo. That ending often makes something sound small; with fruit, rabito can name the short stalk or stem.

example.es: Quitó el rabito de la fresa.
example.en: She removed the strawberry's little stem.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’

Cuente is a special form of contar used when the idea is doubted or not presented as a fact. In contar como, contar means to qualify as something rather than to count numbers or tell a story; the ordinary present form is cuenta.

example.es: Dudo que eso cuente como ayuda.
example.en: I doubt that counts as help.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something counts or qualifies as a particular category?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of contar, then como and the category or description.
cards.noteEn: Contar changes for the person, thing, and time: cuenta, contó, contará, or cuente. Como stays unchanged and has no written accent. Together, contar como is about classification, not counting numbers or telling a story.

cards.answerEn: as; completes contar como, “to count as”
cards.noteEn: After a form of contar meaning to qualify, como introduces the category or description that applies. It has no written accent in this use.

cards.answerEn: take off; remove from yourself (informal command)
cards.noteEn: Quita is the positive command of quitar for one familiar listener. Te attaches to the end because the listener removes something from themself, and the written accent keeps the original stress.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.promptEs: quitarse el abrigo · quitarse los zapatos
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes off their own clothing?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of quitarse, then el, la, los, or las and the clothing item.
cards.noteEn: The short part me, te, se, or nos identifies the wearer, so Spanish normally uses the definite article—the words el, la, los, or las—instead of a possessive such as mi or tu. The verb changes for the person and time: me quito el abrigo, se quitó la chaqueta. In a positive command to one familiar person, te attaches at the end: quítate los zapatos.

cards.answerEn: your here; Spanish uses los before clothing whose wearer is clear
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses el, la, los, or las rather than a possessive before clothing when a verb or a short word such as me, te, or se already identifies the wearer. Los is the masculine plural form.
